title: sandhi plainly
hook: a famous Gita line about the unreal, with no 'un-' to be seen
tomorrow: one hidden a, and two schools read a line opposite ways?

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhi plainly in a seer's title: raja plus rishi joining as rajarshi. Today, a join that leaves almost no trace.

Here's an odd thing about a famous line. It's about the unreal, and there's no un- anywhere in it. The Gita, chapter two: nasato vidyate bhavo, nabhavo vidyate satah. Roughly: of the unreal, there is no being; of the real, there is no non-being. Two negatives in each half. Yet look at the words, and each half seems to hold only one: na, not. So where did the other one go? And how would a reader ever find it?
screen: `A LINE ABOUT THE UNREAL.` → `NO 'UN-' IN SIGHT.` → `WHERE DID IT GO?`

segments.voice: Start with a small rule. When a word ending in a meets a word starting with a, the two short a's melt into one long one. Na, not, plus asti, is, gives nasti: is not. Now the clue. Na on its own is short. So when a reader meets na with a long a, running straight into more of a word, something may have been swallowed. In this line, it's a second not. Sanskrit can turn a word into its opposite with a short a in front. Sat, the real, being. Asat, the unreal. Bhava, being. Abhava, non-being. So nasato is na and asatah: not, of the unreal. Nabhavo is na and abhavah: not non-being. The a that means un- melted into the a of na, and left only a longer vowel behind. Undone, the line reads: na asatah vidyate bhavah, na abhavah vidyate satah. Panini's rule for it is short: like vowels, joined, become long. Here's a habit worth keeping. When a word in a verse runs a long a straight after na, try splitting it twice: na and the word, then na and the word with a short a in front. Often only one of the two makes sense. And the line's shape was a hint all along. The halves mirror each other, unreal and real, being and non-being. The hidden a's are what make the mirror. That's a reader's whole trick in small: notice what's slightly off, then ask what it's hiding.
screen: `A PLUS A: ONE LONG A.` · `NA IS SHORT. A LONG ONE IS A CLUE.` · `ASAT: A SHORT A MEANS UN-.` · `THE HALVES MIRROR EACH OTHER.` · then, large: `TWO NOTS IN EACH HALF.`

segments.voice: If there's paper nearby, write nasato on one line and na plus asatah under it; then nabhavo, and na plus abhavah. Look at the two versions side by side, the joined and the undone, and notice which one the eye prefers. Then set the pen down and rest with the breath.
Sandhi plainly: the joins between words. Today, two short a's melting into one long one, and a not hiding inside it. Two nots, and only one on show.
For the road: sandhi plainly, and a long a might be keeping a short one. Until tomorrow.
